newsitem.title: USA: NBC oper net seen rising 10-15 pct in '97.
newsitem.headline: NBC oper net seen rising 10-15 pct in '97.

text.p: General Electric Co's NBC Inc unit expects operating profits to jump 10 to 15 percent in 1997, according to NBC sources and Wall Street analysts.

The projections were disclosed on Thursday, when top GE and NBC officials met with Wall Street analysts. The session was closed to the press, and NBC officials declined to provide details of the session.
According to one analyst, who declined to be identified, "It was a big pep rally. These guys played up the fact that they're kicking everyone's butt."
While GE does not detail operating profits at its units, NBC contributed $5.23 billion of $49.57 billion in total 1996 revenues.

NBC Chief Financial Officer Warren Jenson said NBC expects 1997 EBITDA -- earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization -- to range from $1.10 billion to $1.15 billion, according to the sources.
Jenson expects NBC's stations group to have pretax profits of more than $500 million this year, with profit margins over 50 percent "and holding," sources said.
Its flagship WNBC-TV station in New York has profit margins of around 66 percent for the latest 12 months. NBC asserted that the station is "the most profitable station in the world."
The Los Angeles station, KNBC-TV, has a 64 percent margin.
NBC officials expect CNBC revenues to range between $225 million and $250 million this year, with pretax profit of more than $100 million.
Officials estimated that all of its diverse cable holdings are currently worth about $4 billion, sources said.

NBC officials argued the advantage to advertisers of the broadcast networks over cable channels, disputing a study by Time Warner Inc's Turner Broadcasting unit that said the bigger cable networks can match the younger-adult demographics captured by the bottom two-thirds of primetime network programming.

The network brass said that in any given week, NBC reaches 74 percent of households in the U.S., and combining all of the other networks, the reach is in the high 60s, while the largest big cable networks, including TNT and TBS, another Turner network, were in the teens.

NBC officials told analysts the network has been progressively shifting its in-house production since 1994. They said the network has gone from producing 16 percent of its primetime programs in house in 1994 to 41 percent this year, excluding its "Dateline" program, which currently runs four nights per week.
Analysts said officials got across the message of a robust network. "They're clearly doing well," said Dennis McAlpine, an analyst at Josephthal Lyon & Ross.
"They're committed to staying number one," said John Reidy at Smith Barney.

Reidy said NBC is building on its consecutive broadcast rights to the Olympics, beginning with the 2000 Summer games in Sydney, to strengthen daytime programming. NBC also owns the rights to all of the Olympics through 2008.
Reidy said the network underscored a "strategy of building on its position on a long-term basis. They built Thursday night, and they're building additional nights."
Analysts said operating results could be higher, if the network chose to cut investment spending.

"A percentage point or two in the growth rate for the year is not going to make much difference," said Reidy. "What you're looking at is broadening and building programming, and adding to the distribution franchise."

Among those who adressed analysts were: Dennis Dammerman, GE senior vice president for finance; Robert Wright, president and chief executive of NBC; Jenson; Don Ohlmeyer, president West Coast; Andy Lack, president of NBC News; Dick Ebersol, president of NBC Sports, and Bill Bolster, president of CNBC.
